title: Balancing local regulations with operational simplicity

opening.headline: When requirements vary by country, we learn how to determine where to establish common standards across all countries and where to allow exceptions.
body: When operating AI services in multiple countries, each country may have different requirements regarding data retention periods, data processing locations, and data storage locations. Following each requirement individually leads to configuration complexity that grows proportionally with the number of countries, and increases the burden of deployment, monitoring, and incident response. Configurations designed to comply with regulations can inadvertently introduce new risks, such as configuration gaps.

In this course, we first examine the control mechanisms provided by Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google in the document. Next, we observe how national requirements are divided into a minimum common configuration and exception configurations, and how compliance costs interact with operational simplicity. We then compare the two design approaches using the same example to establish guiding principles.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Requirements by country can be analyzed and categorized into a minimal common configuration and exception configurations.
Both compliance costs and operational simplicity can be evaluated to determine which is more appropriate.

screens.title: Different configurations across countries lead to various outcomes.
screens.lead: First, let's look at the scenario when we divide the configuration by country.

visual.alt: Four country-specific cards are stacked on the left, while the operational burden list grows on the right.
labels: European entity: process location within the region

paragraphs: Let's assume a company operates AI services in three countries. The Korean subsidiary must have a short data retention period, the U.S. subsidiary must restrict data processing to within the United States, and the remaining subsidiary only needs the default processing location. The simplest approach is to create separate configurations for each country.

However, every time the configuration is added, an additional deployment pipeline, permission policy, inspection item, and incident response procedure are created. Administrators must remember different values for each country, and they may inadvertently omit identical changes in one location when modifying settings elsewhere. The configuration designed to comply with regulations inadvertently introduces a new risk of configuration omissions.

On the contrary, applying the strictest requirements to all countries at once reduces the configuration to a single standard, but weaker countries end up bearing additional costs and functional limitations. The single question this lesson addresses is: up to what point should requirements be common across all countries, and from where should national exceptions be allowed?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: When the number of configurations increases from two to six, the number of settings that need to be checked does not simply triple; it also increases alongside the number of possible mismatched combinations.

screens.outro: First, let us consider whether the same configuration can be applied across all countries.

screens.title: Can the same configuration be applied across all countries?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Can the same configuration be applied across all countries?
items.answer: It is possible. If a configuration exists that satisfies the requirements of all countries, it may be unified into one. However, we must first determine whether such a configuration exists, and if it does, whether the cost of implementing it is reasonable to bear. This course addresses the order of judgment in this process.

items.prompt: The data our service handles belongs to users in a particular country—where should it be processed and stored?
items.answer: The requirements depend not only on the user's country but also on the location where data is processed and where it is stored. The Claude API documentation separately explains the location where inference takes place and the location where data is stored as two independent settings. Therefore, processing and storage locations must be examined separately.

items.prompt: What do we lose if we apply the most stringent requirements of one country to all nations?
items.answer: The setup is simple, but comes at a cost. For example, if you restrict processing location to within the United States, you'll have to pay 1.1 times the standard rate with Claude API, and the range of supported models will be limited. The key point is that you pay the same fee for countries where there is no actual need.

screens.outro: Now we will verify what actual controls the provider's documentation offers.

screens.title: Four axes by which regulations become configuration items
screens.lead: Compare how each provider controls learning, retention, processing, and storage locations by selecting each tab.

tabs.label: OpenAI
tabs.body:
**Learning Usage**: The documentation states that data sent via API is not used for model training unless explicitly agreed to be shared.

**Retention**: Abuse monitoring logs are retained by default for up to 30 days. To exclude customer content from these logs, customers must obtain either Zero Data Retention or Modified Abuse Monitoring approval.

**Scope**: Applies to organizations or projects, requiring prior approval and acceptance of additional requirements.

tabs.label: Google
tabs.body:
**Learning Usage**: No AI/ML model shall use customer data for learning or fine-tuning without prior authorization or instruction.

**Data Processing and Storage Location**: Data is processed and stored only within the specified region. Exceptions include data labeling tasks and experimental or preview feature phases. The Agent Platform does not support global locations.

**Applicable Unit**: Region; when creating a dataset or retrieving a model, the region must be specified.

tabs.label: Anthropic
tabs.body:
**Retention**: Conversation content is not retained by default. However, Covered Models require retention for 30 days.

**Processing Location**: For each request, `inference_geo` specifies either `"global"` (default) or `"us"`. Workspace default settings can also be set.

**Storage Location**: The workspace geo is determined when the workspace is created and cannot be changed afterward.

**Applicable Unit**: Requests and workspaces.

tabs.label: Compare at a glance
tabs.body:
All three companies provide controls to address their respective requirements. However, the names and application scopes differ. OpenAI uses organizational or project-level approvals, Google uses region-specific settings, and Anthropic employs request-level parameter settings and workspace configurations for control.

Therefore, when translating country-specific requirements into controls, it is necessary to simultaneously define "which company and which unit will enforce the control." The control locations vary by company, even for the same requirement.

screens.outro: Now that we know the control mechanisms, let's reorganize the country-specific requirements into a table with common and exceptional entries.

screens.title: Table dividing country-specific requirements into common and exceptional cases
screens.lead: Switch between the two states to verify how the same requirement is restructured in different forms. The table below shows the example assumed in this lesson.

visual.alt: The country-specific requirements are divided into two groups: the minimum common configuration and the exception configuration.

states.label: Per-country individual configuration
states.body:
If Country A, B, and C each list their respective requirements separately, the configuration becomes three instances. The assumed requirements are five in total: learning use prohibition, minimal preservation, access log retention are required by all three countries, while processing location restriction and storage location fixation are required only by Country B.  

Thus, three of the configuration instances each repeat the same three items three times. Whenever one element is modified, all three corresponding elements must be updated simultaneously, and if any one is omitted, compliance with that country's regulations is compromised.

states.label: Common + Exceptions
states.body:
All three items required by every country are grouped together as the **minimum common configuration**. These include learning prohibition, minimal preservation, and access log retention.

Processing location restrictions and storage location fixation, required only by Country B, are designated as **exceptional configurations**. Exceptional configurations are defined as overriding the common configuration, with each exception including a rationale clause and designated responsible party.

The more extensive the common configuration, the fewer exceptions there are; conversely, the more exceptions exist, the greater the scope of review. Processing location controls are implemented as provider-supplied mechanisms, such as Anthropic's `inference_geo` or Google's region specification. Google's documentation advises users to select a region close to them but to verify whether the desired features are supported in that region—this criterion becomes the basis for evaluating exceptional configurations.

screens.outro: Since classification criteria have been established, we will compare the costs of making common parts thick versus thin.

screens.title: The trade-off between compliance costs and operational simplicity
screens.lead: Adjust the number of sliders to 1, 3, and 6, and examine whether compliance costs and operational simplicity increase or decrease. These values represent scenarios illustrating trends.

visual.alt: Two gauges that move in opposite directions: compliance costs increase with configuration size, while operational simplicity decreases.
labels: Compliance costs (burden passed on by countries with weak requirements)
Operational simplicity (ease of inspection, deployment, and incident response)

stops.body: This is a scenario where a single configuration meeting the strictest requirements is applied across all countries. Since deployment, monitoring, and incident response are all handled in a single cycle, operational simplicity is maximized. In contrast, countries with weaker requirements also incur additional costs and functional limitations. For example, US-only inference in the Claude API costs 1.1 times the standard rate.

This is a case where the configuration is divided according to the number of countries. Each country bears only the necessary share, thus reducing unnecessary costs. However, the deployment pipeline, authorization policies, and compliance checks are duplicated three times, leading to a decrease in operational simplicity. There is also the burden of aligning the same values across three locations.

This is done on a per-national and environmental combination basis. While compliance costs are the lowest, operational simplicity is also the lowest. It becomes difficult to determine which configuration is the standard when settings are misaligned, and with a large number of inspection targets, the risk of omissions increases.

The two values are pulled in opposite directions. Google's Well-Architected perspective also advises to balance security, cost, and operational excellence together. Therefore, the goal is not to maximize one side, but rather to minimize the number of components while satisfying essential requirements.

screens.outro: Since we've verified the behavior of two values, let's solve the same case using two different approaches.

screens.title: Explanation 1: Achieve unification in accordance with the most stringent requirements.
screens.lead: The instructor explains the case step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Check case
steps.body: This service operates in three countries, with one country requiring the inference processing location to be restricted within the United States, while the other two countries do not have such a requirement. Let us consider this case by aligning it with the most stringent requirement.

steps.title: Uses the most strict value by default
steps.body: Assign `inference_geo` to `"us"` for all countries' requests. Setting this value causes inference to run only on U.S. infrastructure. The configuration is reduced to one.

steps.title: Set it in one go in the workspace
steps.body: Parameters may be omitted depending on the call code. Anthropic provides a method to restrict geo access in a workspace to `allowed_inference_geos` and to set a default value when a request lacks a value using `default_inference_geo`. This setting can be configured in the `data_residency` field of the Console or Admin API.

steps.title: Calculates cost impact
steps.body: For models after Claude 4.6, US-only inference incurs a 1.1 multiplier on all standard rates—input tokens, output tokens, cache writes, and cache reads. This 1.1 multiplier also applies to traffic from the two countries not requiring such service. You should expect to pay an amount equal to 1.1 times your total usage.

steps.title: Verify the support model scope
steps.body: `inference_geo` is supported in models after Claude 4.6. Sending this parameter to earlier models such as Claude Opus 4.5 or Claude Haiku 4.5 results in a 400 error being returned. This indicates that a unified configuration narrows the range of model selection.

steps.title: judgment
steps.body: The configuration is simplified to one, making inspection and deployment easier and reducing the risk of omission. In exchange, all countries must bear a cost 1.1 times higher, and the scope of available models is limited. Unified deployment is a good choice if this trade-off is acceptable.

screens.outro: Having verified the benefits and compensation on one end, let's now analyze the same case by country.

screens.title: Explanation 2: Organized by country
screens.lead: For this example, we keep only countries with requirements as an exception. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

visual.alt: A single layer of exception configuration stacked on top of the minimal common configuration.
labels: Minimum common configuration: learning usage restrictions, minimal preservation, access log retention
Exception configuration: Country B workspace, processing location us

steps.title: Define the minimal common configuration
steps.body: First, we collect the items that all three countries must adhere to: learning usage restrictions, minimal preservation, and access log retention. This set applies uniformly across all workspaces.

steps.title: Find the places where exceptions are needed
steps.body: Only one country requires processing to remain within the United States. Apply an exception only to that country's workspace. With Anthropic, this means setting `default_inference_geo` to `"us"` for that workspace.

steps.title: Exceptions only differ in the details.
steps.body: Exception configuration lists only the values that differ from the common configuration. If you copy the entire common configuration, you risk accidentally modifying the common values while overlooking the exception configuration. By listing only the differences, the exception configuration remains small and clearly shows what has changed.

steps.title: Records the basis and responsible party.
steps.body: Record the basis clause and responsible party for each exception. This record is necessary to determine later whether the basis has been removed. Exceptions remaining without basis only increase the inspection burden.

steps.title: Reduces exceptions through regular inspections
steps.body: Regularly review the exception list and absorb or remove exceptions whose rationale has disappeared. As exceptions decrease, the configuration count reduces and operational simplicity increases.

steps.title: judgment
steps.body: Two countries without requirements can operate with a cost only 1.1 times that of U.S.-exclusive inference, while continuing to use their previous models. Instead, they incur the burden of managing exception configurations, and as exceptions increase, the inspection burden grows. The core of this approach is maintaining exceptions in a small, documented state.

screens.outro: Having examined both approaches, I will now summarize the principle to determine which one to establish as the foundation.

screens.title: Decision Principle: As strict as possible, with exceptions only when necessary
screens.lead: We consolidate the two interpretations into a single line of reasoning. Read them in order and apply them to your own structure.

paragraphs: **Step 1: Check if strict unification is feasible.** When applying the most stringent configuration to all countries, verify whether the additional costs and functional limitations can be tolerated. For example, assess whether the cost—1.1 times that of US-only inference—and the restriction to Claude 4.6 or later models falls within an acceptable range.

**Step 2: Unify if feasible.** Reducing the number of configurations simplifies deployment, inspection, and incident response, while also lowering the risk of configuration omissions. When there is only one configuration, there will be no confusion about which value serves as the baseline.

**Step 3: If unable to handle, maintain the common baseline and minimize exceptions.** The minimum common configuration applicable to all countries is retained unchanged, with exception configurations added only to countries having specific requirements. Each exception must be documented with its rationale and responsible party and included in regular audits.

Compliance is the foremost condition to be upheld in all these judgments. Reducing the number of components is a goal pursued within the scope of maintaining compliance. Essential requirements must not be omitted simply because they appear trivial.

callout.label: Judgment criteria
callout.text: When unifying, can we afford the costs and constraints, or is the burden of managing exceptions smaller? We choose based on these two questions.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded or graded.
checks.q: Access log retention is required by all countries, while processing location restrictions are required by only one country. In the common+exception approach, how should these two be arranged?
options: Both requirements are left as country-specific exceptions, each managed separately by the respective country.
Access logs are kept at the minimum common configuration, while processing location restrictions are defined in exception configurations on top of that.
Both requirements are applied equally to countries with no requirements, being included in the minimal common configuration.
Place location restrictions in the common configuration and keep access logs in an exception configuration.
checks.explain: All items required by every country are grouped into a minimum common configuration, while items required by only some countries are separately placed in an exception configuration that overrides the common configuration.

wrong.0: If common requirements are excluded, the number of configurations and the scope of inspection unnecessarily increase.
wrong.2: Being forced to accept additional costs and functional limitations even for countries with no requirements results in a lack of exception minimization and imbalance.
wrong.3: Including mandatory items required by only some countries in the common requirements burdens countries with no such requirements, while excluding items required by all in exceptions increases the risk of omission.

checks.correctFeedback: Yes. We have distinguished between common requirements and requirements from some countries.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Think about it again. The criterion is what several countries are requesting.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded or graded.
checks.q: Consider the procedure for organizing by country in the correct order.
items: Defines a minimal common configuration, including learning user restrictions, minimal data retention, and access log preservation.
Apply exception configurations only in the workspace of countries that need to bundle processing locations.
The exception configuration includes only values different from the common configuration to minimize differences.
Regularly review the exception list and absorb those exceptions that no longer have valid justification.
checks.explain: It is a process of first defining common bases, then adding exceptions only where necessary, keeping those exceptions small and regularly reducing them.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. Start with the common configuration and gradually reduce exceptions.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Let's take a closer look at the sequence. The common base must be established first.

glossary.def: A fundamental control suite applicable without exception to all countries. This includes learning usage restrictions, minimal preservation, and access log retention.
Additional or modified values overlaid on the common configuration due to requirements from a specific country. The basis clause and responsible party are recorded together.
Direct costs incurred to satisfy requirements and functional constraints. The price multiplier of location-bound inference is an example.
The configuration count is low, making deployment, inspection, and fault response relatively easy.
This is a parameter used in the Claude API to specify the location where inference is executed per request as either "global" or "us".

misconceptions.myth: Safety requires separately designing configurations for each country.
misconceptions.fact: Having common requirements grouped together reduces the risk of configuration omissions. As the configuration grows, the number of combinations that may diverge from the inspection scope also increases.

misconceptions.myth: When unified strictly, it is always optimal.
misconceptions.fact: Unification simplifies the configuration but comes at a cost. First, verify the impacts such as cost multiplier and support model limitations.

misconceptions.myth: The control of the three providers is the same, differing only in name.
misconceptions.fact: The application units differ. They are divided by request, workspace, region, organization, or project approval, so separate determination is required as to where compliance will be enforced.

closing.lead: This summarizes the core content of the class.
points: If unification is difficult, place exception configurations on top of the minimal common configuration.
Compliance costs and operational simplicity are evaluated together.
Exceptions are assigned with rationale and responsible party, and are periodically reduced.
closing.reflectionLead: The questions below are for your own reflection only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What are the country-specific exceptions in our organizational structure, and do these exceptions still have valid basis today?
